description: Hi my name is Grayson , I’m a space enthusiast with a huge passion for exploration, astrophysics, and the mysteries of deep space. 🌌 I’m fascinated by the universe, from black holes and neutron stars to distant galaxies, cosmic phenomena, and the possibility of discovering things we’ve never imagined.
summary:
Project: Horizon is a retro 8-bit space game that brings NASA’s abandoned equipment back to life. It runs in any web browser, with no install.

1) Game objective
Free Roam: fly through the solar system and find and scan all 8 abandoned NASA artifacts.
Mission mode: complete historic missions by launching, surviving Mars entry, releasing the parachute, landing safely, then exploring the Moon and Mars.

2) What you do
Fly a spacecraft between planets and scan artifacts such as Apollo 11’s Tranquility Base, the Viking 1 lander and the Opportunity rover.
Read each artifact’s mission file: launch date, timeline, where it is now and its cause of death.
Handle the landing challenges yourself: the parachute release and the engine burn.
Walk the surface or drive a rover.

3)Why it matters
These machines carry real lessons about engineering, failure and discovery.
A game can teach them to people who would never read a mission report.
details:
Project: Horizon is a retro 8-bit space game that turns NASA’s abandoned equipment into something you can explore. It runs in the browser from a single HTML file.

What it does and how it works: Players pilot a craft through a pixel-art solar system in two modes. In Free Roam, you cruise past the planets and scan abandoned NASA artifacts. Examples are Apollo 11’s Tranquility Base, the Viking 1 lander and the Opportunity rover. Each scan opens a “mission file” card with the launch and arrival details, a timeline, where the hardware is now, and its cause of death. For example, Viking 1 was lost to a faulty software command sent from Earth. In Mission mode, players relive historic missions on Mars and the Moon. They launch, survive Mars entry, time the parachute release, fire the landing engine, then walk the surface or drive a rover.

Benefits and impact: The game teaches real space history through play rather than a textbook. It shows that exploration leaves things behind, and that each failure taught engineers something. We want players to remember these machines and the people who built them.

Tools, languages and software: We built the game with HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript and CSS. All graphics are pixel art drawn in code with the Canvas 2D API, and the sound effects, engine sound and music come from the Web Audio API. The result is a lightweight game that needs no install and runs on almost any device with a browser. We used Python and Node.js scripts to build and test it, Playwright (headless Chromium) for automated testing and for capturing gameplay footage, and FFmpeg to edit the intro video.

Creativity: Instead of a single-objective game, we built a “digital museum” you fly through. Each artifact card reads like a case file, with archive-style photo effects and a neon sci-fi HUD. We designed the pacing to be calm and readable, with slow walking and dialogue that only advances when you press Space.

Factors considered: Historical accuracy to NASA data, accessibility (a controls screen, a pause menu and a hide-UI key), and keeping the game playable by anyone at a hackathon booth within a minute.
Use of AI: ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude
